# Statistical Inference: Inferring the Expectation and Variance of a Population

```{r pressure-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="It's finally time for statistics.", out.width="80%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/stand_back.jpg")
```

In the last few chapters, you have gone on a whirlwind tour, and you should be very proud of the things you have learned. We started at the very basics - discussing sample spaces and the stuff we call probability. Next we talked about **random variables** and descriptions of their probability distributions. We talked about both continuous and discrete random variables, and importantly, we learned about the expectation and variance of those random variables. At many moments throughout this (perhaps long; although hopefully exciting) adventure you may have asked yourself why all this is so relevant. We are behavioral researchers after all! We aren't stupendously interested in probability or the concept of randomness. But, as you will see, these concepts will help us unlock a wonderful capacity to study the things that we love to learn about.

It is therefore prudent to return to the very first thing we talked about in chapter 1 of this book - behavioral research. Suppose we are conducting descriptive research of a group of interest. We conduct some sort of measurement with an randomly selected individual or creature (heretofore also referred to as individuals for simplicity and sympathetic reasons) from this group. With that measurement in hand, suppose we repeated such an experiment, e.g., selection of an individual via some random process for measurement. We would undoubtedly find that the value of our measurement might change from person to person. In this sense, we will treat the thing we are measuring as  *random variable*. This random variable will have some sort of distribution or description of its randomness. However, unlike the previous chapters of this book, we will have very little idea as to the nature of that distribution. We won't know its form, expectation, and/or variance. 

For the purposes of our discussion here, these random variables and their corresponding probability distributions are referred to as *populations*. The probability distribution describes all the likely (and unlikely) values within the population of interest. For example, if we were studying the height of cats (it's Caturday as I write this), we might find that cats who are 1 inch tall are very rare and cats who are about 11 inches tall to be relatively frequent. Note that the aforementioned definition is different from the (also valid) definition that you might find in other books. In those books they refer to populations as groups of humans or animals that you hope to study - not as measurements/values and their corresponding probability distribution. Of course these are two meanings that are useful in certain contexts. In this circumstance we shall use the former.

As we will learn later, we will be better able to describe the population we are interested in if we gather more than a single *observation* of our measure. Simply measuring one cat's height would be absolutely insufficient to learn about the population of interest, for example. Suppose we called our measure of cat height - $X$. To get a better sense of the distribution this variable, we would endeavor to randomly seek out multiple cats and measure their height. Throughout this difficult, adorable, and scratchy process, it would be our hope that the random process for selecting cats is truly random - e.g., every single cat or individual has equal likelihood to be selected for measurement. In the case of a *random sample* like this, we would now have several random variables $X_1$, $X_2$, $X_3$, ... , $X_n$ for the $n$ cats we hope to measure. These will each have the same probability distribution because they are each from the same population of cat heights. If we further believe/know that these random variables are independent, then we would call the set of random variables *independent and identically distributed* or i.i.d.

Of course, these are random variables, because as we pondered way back in chapter 1, the actual realized value of each of the above random variables may change from sample to sample. Thus, to reduce some ambiguity, we will again refer to a particular realization of our sample in lower case letters. In this case, we would write $x_1$, $x_2$, $x_3$, ..., $x_n$ to refer to a single outcome of our sampling procedure. Next comes the fun part. In this section we are going to learn about how we might use this sample to make inferences about the population of interest. In particular, we will learn about how we might infer the expectation and variance of the population. As you will see, this starts with **describing** our sample.

## Describing a sample
Suppose we are happiness researchers, and we are interested in describing the average happiness level of folks in the Sacramento area. We gather data from a random sample of individuals living in this city on a well validated happiness inventory. The inventory yields a final happiness score of 0 to 100. We select 10 people at random to take the inventory. That is, we have 10 random variables - $X_1$, $X_2$, ... , $X_{10}$ - and after we conduct our random sample we shall get 10 realized values - $x_1$, $x_2$, ... , $x_{10}$. After an arduous research journey, although perhaps less scratchy than working with cats, we gather our 10 realized measurements or **observations**

$$
63.50, 37.5, 59.3, 53.5, 39.5, 54.9, 49.4, 55.6, 69.3, 47.3
$$
The first thing we shall want to do with our sample is *describe* it. In practice, it is nice to have some summary numbers that take all the information in our sample and reduce it to something a little more ingestable. One thing we'd like to calculate is some measure of the *middle* of our sample of values, and another thing we'll be interested in is describing how much they *vary* from observation to observation. We will focus on the first and the move to variability later in the section. We'll close out with a couple of ways to visualize your data.

Measures of the middle of a sample are frequently referred to as **measures of central tendency**. There are three such measures frequently taught in behavioral statistics books - the mean, median, and mode. Let's talk about the mean first. Suppose for a moment that we treated our sample as a uniform discrete distribution. That is, for each observation in our sample with size $n$, we assign a probability of $1/n$ to each value. So, for our current sample we would have a distribution like this:

$$
p(x) =
\begin{cases}
1/10 & x_1 = 63.50 \\
1/10 & x_2 = 37.5 \\
1/10 & x_3 = 59.3 \\
1/10 & x_4 = 53.5 \\
1/10 & x_5 = 39.5 \\
1/10 & x_6 = 54.9 \\
1/10 & x_7 = 49.4 \\
1/10 & x_8 = 55.6 \\
1/10 & x_9 = 69.3 \\
1/10 & x_{10} = 47.3
\end{cases}
$$
